prompt: For classes of finite simple graphs, what is the relation between bounded clique-width and bounded twin-width?

answers.text: Bounded clique-width implies bounded twin-width; the converse fails, for example on square grids.
answers.explanation: Clique-width bounds yield twin-width bounds. Square grids have uniformly bounded twin-width but unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width, but not conversely.
answers.explanation: The implication is in the other direction; square grids refute the proposed implication.

answers.text: The two boundedness properties are equivalent.
answers.explanation: Square grids have bounded twin-width and unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Neither boundedness property implies the other.
answers.explanation: Every class of bounded clique-width has bounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded clique-width implies bounded twin-width only for sparse classes.
answers.explanation: The implication holds also for dense graphs; no sparsity hypothesis is needed.

answers.text: Bounded clique-width implies bounded twin-width only for hereditary classes.
answers.explanation: The parameter bound applies to individual graphs and hence to any class, without a closure hypothesis.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width for all bipartite classes.
answers.explanation: Square grids are bipartite and still have unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width for all planar classes.
answers.explanation: The square-grid counterexample is already planar.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width for all classes of maximum degree at most four.
answers.explanation: Square grids have maximum degree at most four.

answers.text: The parameters are numerically equal on every graph.
answers.explanation: Even a clique with at least two vertices has twin-width zero and clique-width two.

sources.title: Bonnet et al. — Twin-width I, §§2–4 (2021 version)
